RagShortTexts: William of Saliceto revolutionized 13th-century surgery at Bologna, rejecting 'laudable.

Variants.Content: William of Saliceto (c. 1210–1277) taught surgery at the University of Bologna and reshaped the way medieval physicians treated wounds. In his Chirurgia, completed around 1275, he challenged the Galenic belief that pus, which he called laudable pus, was a sign of healing and natural ripening of a wound. He argued that suppuration caused harm to the tissue and slowed recovery, so the surgeon should aim for clean closure. He advocated sharp scalpel incisions to drain abscesses and clean wounds, in place of the indiscriminate use of the hot cautery irons that had long been standard. His work reunited internal medicine with manual surgery and helped move the craft from the barber's shop toward a learned academic discipline.
Italian-trained surgeons employed delicate arterial ligatures and wine antiseptic dressings, drastically improving battlefield survivability.
